items.title: How to choose the right journal for your manuscript
items.summary: A step-by-step checklist for shortlisting a suitable, genuinely indexed journal before you submit.
items.body:
Choosing the right journal is one of the biggest factors in whether your paper is accepted quickly. Use this checklist before you submit.

## 1. Match the scope
- Read the journal's *Aims & Scope* page and compare it with your topic and study type.
- Look at 5–10 recent articles: are they similar to yours in subject and design?

## 2. Verify indexing yourself
Never rely only on the journal's own website. Check the official sources:
- **Scopus**: search the title on the Scopus Sources list.
- **PubMed / MEDLINE**: search the NLM Catalog for the journal and its current indexing status.
- **Web of Science**: search Clarivate's Master Journal List.
- **DOAJ** for open-access journals.

## 3. Check the practical details
- Article processing charge (APC) and any waiver policy
- Average time to first decision and to publication
- Word limits, reference style and accepted article types

## 4. Read the author guidelines carefully
Format your manuscript exactly as the journal asks. Many papers are returned before peer review only because of formatting.

Need help shortlisting journals for your paper? [Send an enquiry](contact.html).

items.title: IMRaD: how to structure a research manuscript
items.summary: What goes into the Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion, and the most common mistakes in each.
items.body:
Most health-science journals expect original research in the **IMRaD** format: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion.

## Introduction
- What is known about the problem, briefly, with recent references
- The gap your study addresses
- A clear aim or objective in the final paragraph

## Methods
- Study design, setting and period
- Participants: inclusion and exclusion criteria, sample size and how it was calculated
- Intervention or exposure, outcomes and how they were measured
- Statistical analysis, and the software used
- Ethics committee approval and informed consent

## Results
- Present findings in the same order as the objectives
- Use tables and figures for detail and do not repeat every number in the text
- Report exact p-values and confidence intervals where possible

## Discussion
- Start with the main finding
- Compare with previous studies, explaining similarities and differences
- Strengths and limitations, honestly stated
- A conclusion that does not go beyond your data

**Tip:** write the Methods and Results first, then the Discussion, and the Introduction and Abstract last.

items.title: Responding to peer reviewers: a practical guide
items.summary: How to write a clear, polite point-by-point response that improves your chances after a revision decision.
items.body:
A *major* or *minor revision* decision is good news: the journal is interested in your paper. How you respond matters.

## Before you start
- Read all comments, then wait a day before replying
- Group comments into: easy fixes, ones needing new analysis, and ones you disagree with

## Writing the response letter
- Thank the editor and reviewers briefly at the start
- Copy **each comment** and write your reply directly below it
- Say exactly what you changed and where (page and line numbers)
- Highlight changes in the revised manuscript, or use tracked changes if the journal asks

## When you disagree
- Stay polite and evidence-based
- Explain your reasoning with references
- Where possible, add a sentence or limitation to the paper to show you considered the point

## Before resubmitting
- Check every comment has a reply
- Keep within the revision deadline, and ask the editor for an extension early if you need one

[Get help with your revision](contact.html).
